stories.title: Aspen Landscapers Let the Bots Do the Paperwork so the Crew Stays on the Lawn
stories.summary: Aspen landscaper Jeff Margulies deployed AI across a dozen parts of his business so his 60-to-70-person crew can stay on the lawn instead of buried in paperwork. Real-time job costing, progress photos, and automated scheduling have helped Good Earth grow sixfold.
stories.extended_summary: Jeff Margulies calls it "tickling the bots." The Aspen landscaper has wired Claude-based AI into roughly a dozen parts of Good Earth Landscaping—from field photos and clock-ins to real-time job costing checked against the budget on the spot. The goal isn't fewer workers; it's keeping his 60-to-70-person crew on the lawn instead of drowning in admin. Since he bought into the company in 2018, Good Earth has grown sixfold, and the paperwork now mostly handles itself.

stories.title: Fracking wastewater as source of critical minerals? North Dakota startup uses AI-engineered proteins to turn a liability into an asset
stories.summary: A North Dakota startup is using AI-designed proteins to pull critical minerals out of fracking wastewater—turning a toxic liability into a national-security asset. HydroBIND's founder wants to give farmers and ranchers something positive from water that's long been their bane.
stories.extended_summary: Fracking wastewater has long been the bane of North Dakota farmers—too salty, too toxic, too much of it. Steve Kemp wants to flip that. His Williston startup, HydroBIND, uses AI to precision-engineer proteins that bind to valuable minerals and only those minerals, pulling critical materials out of produced water that the country desperately needs for EV batteries and electronics. "Boy, wouldn't it be nice if we could develop something positive for the landowners and the farmers and the ranchers," Kemp says. It's a liability-to-asset play sitting right in the heart of the Bakken.

stories.title: From payphone to playtime: Grocer’s Daughter gives old technology new life
stories.summary: A Michigan chocolate shop turned an eBay payphone into an AI-powered mystery: pick up the receiver and interrogate nine characters—including Mr. Sprinkles the Cat—to solve who destroyed a chocolate cake.
stories.extended_summary: Pick up the payphone outside Grocer's Daughter Chocolate in Empire, Michigan, and an AI operator answers—begging for your help solving a crime: someone destroyed a chocolate cake. Dial 1 through 9 to interrogate nine suspects, each with a different attitude and alibi, including the Chef and Mr. Sprinkles the Cat. Co-owner DC Hayden bought the phone on eBay and built the whole thing with a tech-savvy friend, using Google Studio characters that respond so naturally you forget you're talking to a robot. Kids figured it out instantly; Hayden had to tweak it to be more intuitive for everyone else. It's a relic of the past rewired into pure neighborhood play.
